nodes.t: The clay map itself. Tap any point in the US to see the soil, how deep the clay sits, its raw colour and a clay potential level with reasons. Everything around it is how people find it, how I count what happens, and getting it onto phones.
Each place I post has two parts: the post that makes someone curious, and the link in it that brings them to the map and counts where they came from.

nodes.s: what every post is made from
nodes.t: One file per clay, every fact traced to a source. Georgeville at Seagrove is the first. Every reel, pin and page below is made from it.

Reels on wildclayhunt made from my own clips of a real dig, town read or test, at most one a week and none in a week when nothing real happened. Each reel follows the same written method and the same voice. Link since Nov 4: wildclayarchive.com/app/instagram.
steps: Nov 5 · What makes a foraging account (rocks, minerals, clay) work on Instagram, pooled across many accounts.
Nov 6 · One real thing from my own clips per reel, made the same way each time.
Nov 6 · Two clays in one bank, Charlotte County, Virginia (the dig of January 8, 2025).
gate: Find the real thing in the clips by eye, with date and county from their metadata. County at most; the spot goes in no file and on no frame.
One claim with the place in it, about something the viewer could find or has seen. The app is not in it.
The site’s own lookup for that ground, a phone-size capture of its panel, every number and caveat in its wording, with URL and date.
The cut, about 30 seconds: ground with the claim, bank close, tool and hand with no words, the lumps, the site’s panel, the find last with www.wildclayarchive.com.
Only the clips’ own sound, each under its shot, a faint woods tone under the stills. No other track.
Check the file: 1080x1920, 30 fps, frames at the cuts, levels, no dashes anywhere.
A draft with caption, shot list, facts and sources, checks and the one decision left to me. I post from the phone.
shape: Posted as it is, no Add audio. The location tag is the county on the first frame.
The claim first, the site’s wording for the level and its caveat, the permission line, one question, the plain address last. No hashtags.
www.wildclayarchive.com/app/instagram, the door the site counts, and the story sticker uses it too. Caption and screen say “the map is at www.wildclayarchive.com”, never “link in bio”.

nodes.t: Three Georgeville pins so far, each linking to that spot on the map. Link since Nov 4: wildclayarchive.com/app/pinterest.
The Georgeville record laid out as a channel, with the map link in the Wild Clay Archive channel. Link since Nov 4: wildclayarchive.com/app/arena.
The Wild Clay Hunt, my weekly newsletter, with its own map link. Link since Nov 4: wildclayarchive.com/app/substack.
A page for every soil series the map rates, 25 state pages and a guide to finding wild clay, so someone searching for clay near them lands on the map.
How the app shows up in my portfolio: one page that tells what it is, where it came from and that it works, for potters, app reviewers and clients alike.
Picked Nov 5: each project gets its own page on the site, and that page is its project map, like this one. The five ideas below can still live inside a map as pieces.
opts: One page built around a short screen recording, then origin, how it works, proof and what’s next.
One real dig start to finish: old map, lead, hole, bucket, fired tile. The app is the tool in the story.
SYSTEM, INPUT, RULES, OUTPUT as the whole page: data in, rules that score a site, clay out.
A grid of fired tiles from clay found with the app, each linked to its spot on the map.
The build log as a public channel, embedded on the site.

nodes.t: Picking a spot and seeing likely clay. Shows what the app does faster than words.
Clay actually dug from a spot the map pointed to, and the fired tile from it. The piece most app portfolios can’t show.
A public copy of this map on the portfolio site: same diagram, read-only, linked from the project list. The same shape repeats for each project.
What happened, read once a week and kept as rows in one table. It helps pick the next clay.
Visitors, lookups, Pro unlocks, where people came from. Latest reading, 30 days to Oct 26: 163 visitors, 34 looked something up, 3 unlocked Pro.
Each link’s taps, leaving out bots, link previews and me.
A campaign per link in each store console, so installs can be counted by place too.
Where the map becomes an app on phones: listings, screenshots, tester invites and the release-day steps.
Live on the App Store since Nov 6, 2026, with the Pro purchase.
The Android build is in closed testing with invited potters.
The steps in order: Apple’s email, switch the App Store link on, post the launch reel, then Google Play when it clears.
